items.title: Overlooked Movies of the 1970s: This Jodie Foster Thriller Came Out the Same Year as 'Taxi Driver'
items.summary: Two-time Oscar winner Jodie Foster had her first-ever top-billed leading role in the 1976 thriller The Little Girl Who Lives Down the Lane, and yet it remains criminally underrated. Now that the movie has celebrated its 50th anniversary in May, it’s high time to break down how this momentous occasion in the history of the Silence of the Lambs star could have become so overlooked, and why that needs to change. Jodie Foster Had a Banner Year in 1976 Ultimately, it makes sense why The Little Girl Who Lives Down the Lane would have slipped through the cracks. After all, it arrived smack-dab in the middle of what was probably the most important year of Jodie Foster’s career, to this day. By the time Little Girl arrived in theaters, Foster had already played important roles in two major releases, starring opposite Richard Harris in the family drama Echoes of a Summer and opposite Robert De Niro in the Martin Scorsese classic Taxi Driver. She played a key supporting role as a 12-year-old sex worker, which earned her her first Oscar nomination, kicking off a career full of major Oscar recognition. Over the years, Jodie Foster earned four additional nominations, for The Accused in 1989, The Silence of the Lambs in 1992, Nell in 1995, and Nyad in 2024, winning for The Accused and The Silence of the Lambs. Taxi Driver was a huge, career-establishing movie for Foster, and it wasn’t her last of 1976. She also had two major movies debut after appearing in The Little Girl Who Lives Down the Lane. In addition to starring in the all-child gangster musical Bugsy Malone (which was nominated for nine BAFTAs, two Golden Globes, and an Oscar, winning five BAFTAs), she co-starred with Barbara Harris in the live-action Disney classic Freaky Friday. While Taxi Driver proved her ability to play mature roles even as an adolescent, Freaky Friday proved that she could still play her age and star in family films. items.title: What You Can Learn from Bong Joon Ho’s 4 Favorite Movies
items.summary: South Korean filmmaker Bong Joon Ho is one of international cinema’s most versatile directors, crafting genre-defying works (including the 2019 Best Picture winner Parasite) in both Korean and English that bring laughs, thrills, and tears while provoking the audience to think about the state of the modern world. However, no filmmaker exists in a vacuum. When Letterboxd recently asked Director Bong about his four favorite movies during a red carpet interview, he didn’t offer any commentary on the titles he picked, but his answers nevertheless exposed a great deal about some of his key influences. Let’s break down those picks, one by one. Deliverance (1972) The first film on Bong Joon Ho’s list was John Boorman’s Deliverance, a controversial release that shocked audiences at the time and still holds its potency. The movie, which was adapted by James Dickey from his own novel, stars Burt Reynolds, Jon Voight, Ned Beatty, and Ronny Cox as four friends who live in the city and decide to go on vacation in rural Georgia, where they are attacked by locals in an onslaught that includes a prolonged scene of sexual assault. Despite, and perhaps because of, its controversial material, the movie was an enormous hit, grossing $46.1 million against its $2 million budget and going on to be nominated for three Oscars, including Best Picture (it lost two to The Godfather and one to Cabaret, which is hardly shameful). One thing that was particularly shocking, and thus effective, about the movie was that it featured major stars in a way that audiences had never seen them before. While Cox and Beatty were unknown quantities at the time, Jon Voight already had Midnight Cowboy and Catch-22 under his belt, while Reynolds was already well known for playing ruggedly masculine roles in movies like Operation C.I.A., Navajo Joe, and Sam Whisky. items.title: The Most Essential Movies of 1999
items.summary: When you think of the greatest movie years of all time, one of the most recent entries people often turn to is 1999. A year that gave us some of the best of genre, independent, and blockbuster filmmaking. Let’s take a look at some of the most essential movies of 1999. The Sixth Sense Often mistaken for a debut, the third feature film from auteur M. Night Shyamalan was such a smashing success upon release that it made him an instant cinematic cultural figure. The film’s iconic quotes are still spoken by audiences today, and the twist ending is difficult to outshine with its brilliance. Beyond all of the elements that people speak about the most, the film remains a stunningly moving portrait of a family paralyzed by grief and mental illness. Haley Joel Osment’s performance as Cole Sear is one of the finest child performances of all time, and shows a character harnessing such a traumatizing curse and using it to spread as much good as possible. For as much as this one still gives us the shivers, it makes our eyes just as misty by the end. Magnolia ‘Magnolia’Credit: New Line Cinema Indie icon Paul Thomas Anderson released his third feature film, Magnolia, in the final weeks of 1999, and it’s the film that many fans of his still say defines his career, which is a tough placement to hold considering his other works. The film functions in an anthology setting with each story becoming loosely connected by unexplained coincidences in the final act. It explores grief, hot-headedness, family, loneliness, and masculinity in a way that feels as if at any moment it will collapse under its own weight and ambition. However, due to the absolutely extraordinary script and direction by Anderson, and career–best performances from actors like Tom Cruise, the film flexes every muscle it has throughout every frame to deliver a truly unique experience upon every viewing. items.title: The 36-Hour Edit That Earned This 'Saturday Night Live' Segment an Emmy Nomination
items.summary: Every week, the editorial team at Saturday Night Live has less than 36 hours to turn raw footage into ready-to-air sketches, but editors Salerno and Makower find this to be the most exciting part of the job. Their now Emmy-nominated season 51 sketch “MAHAspital (The New Pitt)” is a perfect example of how, even under such tight timelines, the team can craft smart, award-worthy satire for today’s audiences. The SNL editors leverage Premiere to streamline their incredibly fast workflows and collaborate on cuts leading all the way up to showtime. On “MAHAspital,” a sketch parodying the intensity of The Pitt and some controversial alternative medicine practices, Salerno and Makower leveraged the Essential Sound Panel to mimic the dramatic tone and intensity of HBO’s medical thriller while creating a stark contrast with the absurdity of the script. With such a rapid turnaround, constant communication is also critical, and Premiere allows the team to collaborate directly within their timelines without interrupting their workflows. Read on for more from Salerno and Makower on crafting satire through precise scene assembly and experimental soundscaping. Christopher, tell us a little bit about your work at SNL. What was your reaction when you first read the script for “MAHAspital?” Christopher Salerno: Working at SNL has always been a privilege. I started as an assistant editor toward the end of Season 43 in 2018 and have since moved into one of the film unit editor roles. This specific sketch, “MAHAspital (The New Pitt),” grabbed me from the moment I read the script. The two ideas fit together so naturally into such an absurd premise that you could tell on the page there was something special there. items.title: Iconic Film Character Intros: Captain Jack Sparrow - How to Steal a Movie in Seconds
items.summary: When you’re asked to think about iconic character introductions, your mind may not immediately shoot to Captain Jack Sparrow. Obviously, the character himself has become a cultural icon, but his absolutely brilliant introduction in the first film of the series, The Curse of the Black Pearl is not talked about nearly enough. Let’s change that. Uniquely Controlled Chaos Our first time seeing Captain Jack Sparrow is atop the sail of what one would probably assume is a behemoth masterpiece of a pirate ship. Except it’s not. Calling it a dinghy would be generous. On top of that, it’s slowly sinking into the sea as Jack tries his hardest to make it to shore with it. He has a makeshift bucket setup trying to offset the water retention to no avail; he’s operating the entire boat by himself, and even if the ship wasn’t sinking, it clearly was not being kept very well for a long time prior. Yet, in the midst of all of this, it seems as if Jack really couldn’t care less about the insanity of the moment. After the singular attempt to dump some water out of the boat, he simply climbs back on top of the sail mast, and rides the sinking boat directly into the dock, stepping off as if nothing bizarre had just occurred. To draw even more attention to himself, the place he’s docking is Port Royal which is as snottily fancy as it sounds. But… He Can Belong Anywhere ‘Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl’Walt Disney Studios Characters around Jack often go back and forth between falling for his schemes and seeing right through him. But one thing is constant during both instances: Jack always thinks he’s fooling everyone all of the time. As he starts totally not suspiciously walking towards the front of the dock and the mainland, everyone is staring in his direction, yet he could not care less. items.title: 10 Best Treasure Hunting Movies of All Time
items.summary: From the 1960s to the 2020s, movies about treasure hunting can be as different from each other as the prize the characters are looking for. It’s not always gold that is dug up, after all. Harrison Ford and Clint Eastwood star as rugged action heroes. There are pirates and outlaws; old legends and holographic maps. Across the following ten best movies about treasure hunting, they can make you feel the excitement of being an adventure-seeker or be a cautionary tale about being consumed by greed and obsession. It's a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World (1963) With a runtime that goes from 163 minutes to 197 minutes depending on the version you watch, this is an epic comedy with car stunts, slapstick humor, and backstabbing. ‘It’s a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World’ (1963)Credit: United Artists Different groups of motorists witness a car crash, where the driver tells them with his dying breath the location of a buried suitcase with thousands of dollars. Jonathan Winters, Mickey Rooney, Ethel Merman, and more insult or brawl one another en route to the seaside park where the money is hidden. Director Stanley Kramer was known for his dramas with social messages, like Guess Who’s Coming to Dinner and Judgment at Nuremberg. He would also make It’s a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World, a movie bursting at the seams with gags and cameos (look out for Buster Keaton and The Three Stooges). There are many ways to explore how greed can corrupt anyone. Kramer did it with action scenes that are as bonkers as the outrageous comedy. items.title: The Kelsey Grammer Rule for Writing Better Dialogue
items.summary: Being a writer is hard, right? Hopefully you're passionate about the story and building interesting characters and doing all the little things you have to do to make a strong script. And then you have to send it out. To actors. Gulp. And actors read a lot of scripts, which is one of the best forms of storytelling education you can get. So they know ball. They can feel when a character leaps off the page, or a story feels alive. So impressing an actor with your work can be a worthy goal, especially because you need to actually attract talent to get something made. Rich Ronat has felt that, and he has some experiences we can learn from today. He's a genre screenwriter with over a decade of produced credits with Lionsgate and Millennium. He wrote a Nicolas Cage/Kelsey Grammer thriller, Grand Isle, American Sicario for Danny Trejo, war movie The Rising Hawk, and Crescent City, which starred Alec Baldwin, Terrence Howard, and Esai Morales. He recently spoke with Film Courage and told a story about Grammer that might help aspiring writers focus their screenplays. Let's call it "the Kelsey Grammer Rule." - YouTube www.youtube.com What Is the Kelsey Grammer Rule? While working on Grand Isle, Ronat says in the interview, the actor invited him over to run lines before shooting. Over gin and tonics, Grammer told him what he was looking for in a screenplay. "Look, I can read a scene once and know if it's the writing's good." He told Ronat that he should be able to memorize a scene after just one read. If he can't, the writing needs work. On this night, the scene they looked at spanned four pages and included a long monologue for the actor. Grammer read it once. They ran the scene, and Grammer gave his verdict. "Okay, your writing's good." Why It Works What a compliment! Granted, this is an extremely experienced actor with decades of theater and television experience under his belt.
